# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive Summary

Public sources describe Conti as a large, professionally organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation rather than a loose collection of independent criminals. The available record portrays a group that developed and maintained ransomware, recruited technical personnel, used affiliates or other third parties for intrusions, and monetized attacks through data theft, encryption, ransom negotiation, and threatened publication of stolen information. The Center for Internet Security (CIS) characterizes the RaaS model as one in which developers lease malware to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The February–March 2022 ContiLeaks disclosures exposed internal communications, organizational practices, technical-development discussions, alleged financial information, and operational-security failures. Rapid7 reported that the initial disclosure included approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs distributed across 393 JSON files, although some material was encrypted and therefore not fully reviewable. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2) CIS’s account of the leaks describes distinct internal functions—including coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, and penetration testers or hackers—and reports that an insider estimated the organization employed more than 60 people in July 2021. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The public attribution record has two separate components. First, the U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice program publicly assesses that the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are linked to Conti and Wizard Spider. It offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government who participate in qualifying malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1) Second, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. The supplied DOJ record does not, however, state that any of these defendants used one of the five Rewards for Justice aliases. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

The strongest conclusion supported by the sources is therefore that Conti was publicly documented as a commercialized, technically staffed RaaS ecosystem, while attribution to specific individuals remains divided between a reward notice naming online aliases and a DOJ case page naming charged defendants. The supplied evidence does not establish a one-to-one identity match between those aliases and defendants.

## Source Assessment and Scope

The sources differ in institutional role and evidentiary character:

| Source | Institutional character | Main contribution | Evidentiary limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rewards for Justice | U.S. government reward and attribution notice | Names five aliases, associates them with Conti/Wizard Spider, and describes the U.S. government’s assessment of the threat | Uses terms such as “believed to be linked”; does not identify the aliases’ legal names in the supplied text |
| Rapid7 | Cybersecurity company threat-research analysis | Describes the ContiLeaks archive, internal chats, technical practices, and operational response | Reports some leaked material as incomplete or unverified; expressly says it did not access exposed remote systems |
| CIS/MS-ISAC perspective | Nonprofit cybersecurity organization and information-sharing network | Explains RaaS commercialization and summarizes organizational findings from the leaks | Relies partly on open-source reporting and interviews rather than a judicial finding |
| DOJ, Middle District of Tennessee | U.S. federal law-enforcement case record | Names defendants, case numbers, charges, plea information, and victim-notification details | Charges are allegations unless and until proven; the page does not provide a complete evidentiary narrative or alias mapping |

This report treats government assessments as assessments, leaked-chat interpretations as reporting, and criminal charges as allegations unless the supplied record expressly reports a plea or conviction. The DOJ page states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

## How Public Sources Describe Conti’s RaaS Model

### Commercial organization and division of labor

CIS describes ransomware commercialization as a shift toward organizational structures resembling legitimate businesses. These structures may include recruiting or human-resources functions, finance and accounting, and personnel who negotiate ransom payments. In the RaaS model, developers provide or lease malware to affiliates, affiliates conduct victim intrusions, and the parties share revenue. CIS identifies a commonly reported split as approximately 70 percent to affiliates and 30 percent to developers, while presenting that split as a general model rather than a finding necessarily applicable to every Conti transaction. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The significance of this model is operational scalability. Initial-access brokers can sell already established access to victim environments, reducing the time that affiliates must spend penetrating networks. Affiliates can then focus on deploying ransomware and pursuing payment, while the core organization can concentrate on developing, testing, and improving the malware. CIS’s MS-ISAC interview explains that this separation can increase the number of potential victims and allow the core operators to offload some operational risk. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The supplied Rewards for Justice page describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked RaaS group that targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. This is a U.S. government characterization; the page does not provide a detailed legal or intelligence basis for the “government-linked” description. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

### Double extortion and victim pressure

The public descriptions consistently identify a double-extortion model. According to Rewards for Justice, Conti operators typically stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations. The ransom process directed victims to contact the actors through an online portal; if payment was not made, the stolen data could be sold or published on a site controlled by Conti actors. The same page reports that ransom demands varied substantially, with some reaching as high as $25 million. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

CIS likewise describes Conti as a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion. The DOJ record describes Conti ransomware as malicious software that affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and elsewhere. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

Rewards for Justice reports a broader figure: more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure, and more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, including more than 290 in the United States. These figures concern operations and organizations, whereas the DOJ’s “more than 900” figure concerns affected entities. Because the sources use different measures, the numbers should not be treated as directly interchangeable. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

### Malware and associated tools

Rewards for Justice associates Conti with Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. The page labels Conti and Wizard Spider as associated cyberthreat organizations and lists those applications as associated malicious cyber applications. The supplied text does not explain the precise relationship between Conti and each listed application; therefore, the listing supports association, not necessarily authorship or exclusive control. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

Rapid7 reports that Conti’s internal discussions addressed ransomware features, encryption of very large files, endpoint-detection testing, command-and-control infrastructure, malicious documents, and methods for delivering ransomware without detection by dynamic analysis. Rapid7 also reports that the group used phishing as one initial-access method. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

## What the Leaks Exposed

### The ContiLeaks disclosure

Rapid7 reports that, on February 27, 2022, the account known as @ContiLeaks released a large collection of internal Conti chat logs after Conti publicly expressed support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 states that some Conti members supported Ukraine, creating internal conflict, and that Conti later revised its public message. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

The initial archive reportedly contained 393 JSON files and approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs. The material included internal communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of exploits and design processes. Rapid7 cautioned that some messages were encrypted, making the available information incomplete. It also reported that later disclosures included usernames, passwords, alleged access details for command-and-control and storage servers, and a file purported to be Conti source code. Rapid7 explicitly stated that it did not access the remote systems and recommended against using the disclosed credentials. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

### Internal departments and personnel

The leaks depicted Conti as a structured organization with specialized roles. CIS, summarizing research on the disclosures, identifies “Coders” who wrote malicious code and integrated technologies; “Testers” who evaluated ransomware against security products; “Administrators”; “Reverse Engineers”; and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted outside the organization. CIS also reports that departments had their own budgets and could borrow funds from one another. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

CIS reports an insider estimate of more than 60 employees in July 2021, primarily coders and testers. It also states that staffing levels changed, including dismissals after internal security breaches. This supports the conclusion that Conti possessed persistent organizational roles and management practices, but the exact headcount should be treated as an insider estimate rather than a verified personnel census. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

### Product development and spending

The leaks showed efforts to improve the ransomware product and its ability to evade security controls. CIS reports that Conti allocated $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license, budgeted several thousand dollars monthly for security and antivirus software used by testers, and redirected reverse engineers in July 2021 toward Windows 11. ([Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

Rapid7 similarly describes Conti as operating like a software company, with technical discussions about feature development, encryption performance, endpoint-detection products, and deployment logistics. Rapid7 also reports that internal chats included salary negotiations, technical coding exercises, product-status discussions, and out-of-office messages. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

Rapid7 reports that the leaked chats identified a primary Bitcoin address allegedly containing more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. This is a reported interpretation of leaked financial information, not a judicially established balance in the supplied evidence. Rapid7 also reports a conversation suggesting possible FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in information relating to Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. Because the material is incomplete and the supplied source characterizes the implication rather than presenting an adjudicated finding, those points should remain allegations or assessments. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2)

## Law-Enforcement Attribution and Defendant Record

### Rewards for Justice aliases

Rewards for Justice names five online aliases: “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis.” It states that malicious cyber actors known by these aliases are believed to be linked to Conti. The page also associates Conti with Wizard Spider and lists Russia as an associated location. The wording “believed to be linked” signals a government attribution assessment rather than a criminal adjudication identifying each alias’s legal identity. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

The reward is up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The supplied page does not say that every person using one of the five aliases has been legally established to satisfy every element of that description. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1)

### DOJ defendants and case status

The DOJ page identifies two cases. Case No. 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The page states that, on September 7, 2023, these defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

Case No. 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. The DOJ page states that he was charged in connection with a conspiracy to deploy Conti, which infected computers and networks and encrypted data. It further reports that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement, and was scheduled for sentencing on September 10, 2026. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

The supplied DOJ record does not identify any of the five Rewards for Justice aliases as belonging to Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko. Nor does it state that the defendants are the same persons described in the Rewards for Justice notice. Accordingly, a responsible attribution report must keep the alias-based and defendant-based records distinct.

## Contradictions, Gaps, and Uncertainty

The sources present different victim and operation counts: Rewards for Justice reports more than 1,000 operations and more than 400 affected organizations, while DOJ reports more than 900 affected victims. These figures may reflect different definitions, reporting periods, or counting methods. The record does not provide enough information to reconcile them definitively. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); S1; [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2); S4)

There is also a temporal distinction between Rapid7’s March 2022 assessment that Conti remained active and significant after the leak and CIS’s later account that the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units in 2022. These statements are not necessarily contradictory: one concerns activity immediately after the leak, while the other concerns later dismantling and fragmentation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); S2; [Center for Internet Security, 2022](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization); S3)

The principal unresolved gap is identity resolution. The available sources link five aliases to Conti but do not connect them to the DOJ defendants. The DOJ page names defendants and charges but does not provide their online aliases. Any assertion that an alias belongs to a named defendant would exceed the supplied evidence.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a concrete assessment: Conti was publicly described as a mature RaaS enterprise whose criminal capacity depended on specialization, affiliate-based operations, technical development, testing, professionalized administration, and double-extortion monetization. The ContiLeaks disclosures materially strengthened that assessment by exposing internal hiring, budgeting, technical-development, and security-testing practices. They also revealed the risks created by centralized communications and poor operational security.

The attribution record is credible but layered rather than complete. Rewards for Justice provides a U.S. government assessment linking “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” to Conti/Wizard Spider and offers a reward for information concerning qualifying malicious cyber activity. DOJ records separately document Conti-related criminal cases against five named defendants, including charges against four defendants and a reported guilty plea by Lytvynenko. The available sources do not establish that the aliases and defendants are identical. That distinction is essential: public attribution to an online alias, a government threat assessment, a criminal charge, and a guilty plea are different evidentiary categories.

Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward. Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward.
